utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I observe that we are more than a quarter of an hour late in sitting. The reason is the delays in bringing the accused to this court. This is not a matter which can simply be overlooked if it's going to happen day after day. It's not simply a matter of inconvenience to the Court, it's a matter in which time is wasted, public and international time and money is wasted. We shall raise this with the Registry and any other appropriate authority to get the matter sorted out. We will sit again until 2.00 in order to catch up. But this can't go on as a normal response day-in day-out; it will inconvenience other trials. So the matter must be resolved. Yes. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's inconvenient for me too because I have to wait from 8.15 onwards, and the reasons aren't linked to anything that I can do. They're out of my -- it's out of my hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We know that. We'll take it up with the authorities. Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution's next witness is Witness B-1486, via videolink. Your Honour, just on a scheduling matter, I will go into the details of this later on, but there's a scheduling change. Witness 1633, who is in The Hague, for reasons I will explain later is -- will not be testifying tomorrow as scheduled. The Prosecution is proposing to advance Thursday's witness, 1493, until -- to tomorrow and then schedule Morten Torkildsen on Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No doubt you could explain why in due course. Yes. Can the registrar come up for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask that a pseudonym sheet be placed on the overhead projector, and I'd ask that it be displayed in such a way that only the witness via videolink can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: B-1486, I'd ask you to take a look --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. He's to take the declaration first. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If you'd like to sit down again. Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I'd ask you to briefly describe your background.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: I was born in Janja. I graduated from university. Up until the beginning of the war in 1992, I worked in my own profession. I grew up in Janja and spent the whole of my life from birth to September 1994 -- 17th of September, 1994 in Janja.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What is your ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: My ethnic background is Muslim. I am a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what is the ethnicity or ethnic make-up of Janja?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Janja was inhabited by the Muslim population. 99 per cent of the inhabitants were Muslim, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you describe for the Chamber, where is Janja with respect to the town of Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Janja is situated 11 kilometres upstream of the Drina River, in comparison to Bijeljina, in relation to Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I want to draw your attention to February of 1992. At that period of time, did you hear reports about armed forces gathering in the vicinity of Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Yes, we did hear about the gathering of armed forces, but they were paramilitary armed forces under the leadership of Arkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, where were they gathering? What are the names of the locations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: They were gathering in villages around Bijeljina on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and also on the territory of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you name any of the villages --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: The places --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: It was the village of Badovinci, which is located in Serbia, and the village of Popovi, which is in fact in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you tell us with as much precision as you can, when did you first hear reports that Arkan and his men were in these locations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: At the end of February and the beginning of March 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to now draw your attention to the beginning of April. Did there come a time when you yourself heard artillery and gunfire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Where we were, we weren't subjected to direct fire or artillery shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could you hear any such fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Yes, we could hear it, but it came from Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: With as much precision as you're able, when did you hear this gunfire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: It was on the 2nd or 3rd of April, 1992, during the Muslim holiday of Bajram.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What did you do in response to hearing this gunfire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: We were in the place we lived in, and we didn't react at all at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did some of your neighbours go into or attempt to go into the town of Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: No, they did not, nor did they go, because the telephone lines were still working, and we were in contact with our relatives in Bijeljina and they gave us some information as to what was going on there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: From Janja, did you hear reports about tanks being on the road between Bijeljina and Janja?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Yes, we did hear about that, and we were able to see some of the tanks in the suburbs, in the periphery between Janja and the first village bordering on Janja.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How many tanks were you able yourself to personally see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: As it's flat land all around the periphery of Janja, we were only able to see three tanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Could you, Mr. Groome, tell the witness not to refer to "we." He's giving evidence about what he saw or heard, and it's very confusing if he talks about "we saw tanks" and all the rest of it. Just keep him, if you would, at what he saw and did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: B-1486, I want to draw your attention to a few days after that. Did you yourself see anybody come to Janja and address people of Janja?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: When Bijeljina was occupied by Arkan and his paramilitary units, Arkan came to Janja with his escort and addressed the citizens of Janja.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And were you yourself present for -- for that address?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I was among the inhabitants present when Arkan personally addressed the citizens of Janja.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did the entire population of Janja appear for that address?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: There was a large mass of inhabitants. I can't give you an exact percentage as to how many people rallied in the centre of Janja on the occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you summarise for the Court what it was that Arkan said to the crowd?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Arkan said that he demanded that the population hand over their weapons, including hunting rifles and any weapons they had, and that he would guarantee the security of the population, that nothing would happen to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did the people of Janja comply with that direction?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: The people of Janja did comply with that demand and handed over all the weapons they had with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did people of -- or did anybody in Janja offer any resistance to Arkan on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: During that entire day and later on, until the population of Janja was actually forced out of their homes, not a single bullet was fired by the Muslim inhabitants in Janja.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: At that point in time, were there any soldiers from the Yugoslav People's Army present in Janja?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: His -- Arkan's escorts came along with Arkan, but at the time there were no soldiers belonging to the Yugoslav People's Army in Janja.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: To get to Janja, would Arkan have had to have travelled the same road upon which you saw three JNA tanks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Arkan took the asphalt road between Bijeljina and Janja, and I saw three tanks on our own fields, our agricultural land.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would he have passed within sight of those tanks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: He must have seen the tanks because those tanks were deployed on a piece of land which belonged to the agricultural concern in the village of Kojcinovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Chamber how your life, your situation, was affected by Arkan's entry into Janja and the municipality of Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: After handing over all the weapons by the Muslim population, the police changed their insignia. Arkan, at the time, told the inhabitants that as of that moment, pound authority in the Bijeljina municipality was in the hands of the so-called Serbian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you lost some of your personal property as a result of the takeover of Janja?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Curfew, as it was called, was introduced. All the telephone lines were cut so that we were not able to communicate with Bijeljina or further afield in the world. Our movements were restricted so that the inhabitants weren't able to leave Janja, going off in any direction, taking any of the roads out.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you have any property taken from you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Gradually. It was gradually taken away, and finally, all my property was confiscated in September 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you personally aware of mosques in Janja that were destroyed in March of 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that. Both the mosques were destroyed, the mosques which had existed in Janja up until then. They were first set fire to, and then later on they were mined.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How many mosques in Janja were destroyed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Two mosques were destroyed in Janja.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were you personally aware of other mosques in the town of Bijeljina that were destroyed after April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: In Bijeljina, all five mosques which had existed up until then were destroyed, and they were all in working order.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I'd like to play an excerpt from a -- a news report which shows some of the destruction of mosques. There's also a portion at the end of the clip which is related to deportation. The clip is only -- it's less than seven minutes long. It may take longer than that to cue it. So with the Court's indulgence, I may just start the clip now for the mosques and let it run through till the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, sounds sensible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, obviously there was a technical problem. I would note, for the record, that it seems to be a current piece of news that was inserted into our transcript, beginning at 9.36.52, [redacted] [redacted]. So I'd ask that be removed from the record. The tape is being re-cued now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we note what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, there seems to be some technical problem. If perhaps we skip it. Perhaps in redirect examination we could correct this problem and, with the leave of the Court, show it then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you very much more in direct?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, I don't, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, rather than waste time, what we'll do is we will deal with the evidence, we'll have cross-examination. If this is working by the end of your direct examination, we'll hear it. If not, we'll come back to it at the end. Of course the accused will have the opportunity of cross-examining on it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If I can just raise a matter. Your Honour, I was waiting to see what happened with the exhibits this morning. I notice that in tab 4 we've got a video clip with commentary, obviously by a journalist, Channel Four News, with a description of events which it seems the Prosecution is intending to put in as part of the video evidence rather than the pictures themselves. In my submission, it should be the pictures themselves that go in in evidence rather than what the journalist says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But how are we to know what the pictures mean unless we have the commentary?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That can be done by Prosecution counsel's description. There's a witness called Ridelmayer, who is a cultural --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. But we're dealing at the moment with specific mosques. He's going to deal at some stage, later on, he's going to deal with a number of mosques.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: He identifies these mosques as well in his report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is objectionable about this particular commentary?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, it's the fundamental point that the journalist who is making the commentary isn't a witness in the case and isn't here to be questioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But what is he saying which you object to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, if we look at the second line, "upheaval caused by the Serbian campaign of ethnic cleansing in Eastern Bosnia." This isn't a description of the geographical places, the locations, that kind of information. This is commentary on the events that this Trial Chamber is dealing with. It's as if the journalist is giving evidence to this Trial Chamber in a remote way and giving his opinions. It's just dangerous evidence, in our submission, to come in in this form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. One suggestion, of course, is that what we simply do is play it because that will tell us what it is and we ignore his comments. Because they're those, as you rightly say, those of a journalist. He's not a witness. He can't be cross-examined. But when he's describing, "This is Bijeljina and this is the mosque," well, presumably that's not going to be objectionable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That's not objectionable. All I do is point out that if the sound is taken out, there is sufficient linkage evidence to inform the Trial Chamber where these places are in the Ridelmayer report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The difficulty is to combine the two. I mean, of course you may have it in front of you, but for those of us who don't, and the fact that it's not going to be given at the same time, and the fact that there's so much evidence in this case, I think would make it convenient probably to play it. But of course we'll hear and consider it. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I proceed with the next set of questions or argument on this point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we'd better hear some -- what would you say about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution certainly isn't offering the commentary for the truth of what the commentator is saying but simply to assist the Chamber. I think it is also worth noting that the destruction of the mosque in Bijeljina was something that received quite a bit of media coverage, which may be important for the Chamber to consider, just the fact that there was media coverage, when considering whether the accused had notice of the events of this nature in Bijeljina. But I agree with Mr. Kay, and the Prosecution is not advancing this evidence for the truth of what the commentator is saying about Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: A solution may be just to remove tab 4, because you'll have the transcript of the proceedings which advise the Trial Chamber what this particular passage of evidence relates to. But the transcript of it has been included as an exhibit at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. That seems to be a sensible compromise. We'll remove tab 4 but we will allow the commentary played. Of course the comments of the journalist, as throughout, are not admissible as to the truth of it, but it will inform us, of course, what we're actually looking at, and we need that. So we'll remove tab 4 but we'll allow the commentary.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: B-1486, I would ask you to look at your monitor. It is Prosecution Exhibit --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we might have a number for exhibits with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, that bundle.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I believe we used 420 yesterday. 21? I believe there were a couple of pseudonym sheets also marked. By our records, it's 423 -- 423 is the next number.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Correction. Our records are showing 422 would be the next number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: So the pseudonym sheet will be 422, and then the binder for this witness will be P423. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: B-1486, I'd ask you to take a look at Prosecution Exhibit 423, tab 1. It is a series of two photographs. Can you please tell us whether you recognise what's depicted in these photographs.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: This is the mosque which used to stand in the centre of Janja and which was destroyed in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The picture on the bottom half of the page, does that indicate the location as it appears today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Today a new mosque is under construction and construction is almost complete, so that today there is a newly constructed mosque here, as of today.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask you to take a look at the next set of photographs. It's Prosecution Exhibit 423, tab 2. Do you recognise what's depicted in these photographs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Yes. This is another mosque in Janja. It is about 500 metres upstream from the mosque we have just seen. This mosque, too, was destroyed in 1993. The bottom photograph shows the present-day situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask you now to take a look at Prosecution Exhibit 423, tab 3. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Do you recognise what's depicted in this -- in these two photographs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: This is a mosque that used to stand in Bijeljina between the youth centre and the court. This mosque was also destroyed in 1993. On this spot today there is a clear space which is fenced in.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd like to now draw your attention to March of 1993. Did there come a time when local Muslim men were being coerced into joining the Army of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: It is correct. They were coerced, especially employees working in companies. They were given two options: Either they should accept a military assignment and go to the front line in order to keep their jobs, or they could give up their jobs if they did not want to accept a military assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were there schools available for the children of Muslim occupants of Janja?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Schools were available, but the curriculum was the curriculum of the then-Yugoslavia, that is, Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you yourself had to leave Janja?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Yes. At one point in time, under psychological pressure, all the inhabitants of Janja had to leave. Before this, they were robbed by military conscripts belonging to the Serbian army and the Serbian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you give us an approximate time of when you left Janja.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: In mid-September 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you please describe the circumstances under which you left.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Everything was taken from us, from agricultural machinery and livestock to houses. Practically everything we owned was first taken from us. And then we were forced to abandon our property. We could no longer dispose of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What happened to your house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: My house was confiscated by -- by a policeman who was a member of the special police.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you know a person by the name of Vojkan?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Yes. He was a well-known person, and he organised the removal of the population of Janja.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was he involved on the day that you left Janja?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. He organised convoys, or rather, he organised transportation as far as a place called Ban Brdo. But afterwards, he also organised the confiscation of all our valuables; gold jewellery, money, anything of value.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, my last questions to you will be after I ask you to view a videotape. I'm going to play that videotape for you now, and I will ask you my questions when it concludes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that it is technically possible now. Apparently it is, Your Honour. I would ask that we revert to the original plan, with the possibility of, on re-examination, showing the video. I have no further questions of this witness at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to what you say and according to the information here, Janja was almost a purely Muslim village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: According to the census of 1991, there were 10.029 Muslims, 217 Serbs, 17 Croats, 179 Yugoslavs, and 123 others. So one could say that 97 or 98 per cent of the village was Muslim.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. I don't know why this is being shown. All right. Yes. Go on. Go on, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct, Mr. 1486, that at the time of these conflicts in late March or early April, as you said, the 2nd or 3rd of April, in that period you held a leading position in a company in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you employed in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it's not correct you were employed in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I have to take a look. You say on page 3 here of your statement, it says in paragraph 2, in the second sentence of paragraph 2: "As I worked in Belgrade, from that moment it became a foreign country. I could not travel there. So after about two months, I was fired from my work." I won't mention the name of the company in order to avoid identifying you. So were you or were you not employed in Belgrade? This is what it says in your statement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: I happened to be in Janja on Bajram when the conflict in Bijeljina broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. 1486, I didn't ask you where you happened to be at that moment. What I asked you was: Did you have a job in Belgrade? Is this correct? Were you or were you not employed in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Yes, I was employed in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Until when did you work in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Until the outbreak of the conflict in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So when the conflict broke out, you stopped going to work in Belgrade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how long had you been employed in Belgrade at that point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Eight years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A full eight years?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In view of your year of birth and so on, you worked in Belgrade as a young man. Did you have any problems in Belgrade because you were a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Not until that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Not until then. But after that, you didn't even go to Belgrade; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So in all your experience, did you ever experience any problems in Serbia as a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that many refugees, including over 70.000 Muslims, fled to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: I'm not aware of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you are aware of the fact that many refugees fled to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say that some sort of paramilitary units arrived in late February, early March. My information, collected by my associates, says that the events you speak of happened in the night of the 31st of March and on the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd of April. Is this correct or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: It's correct as far as Bijeljina is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how these conflicts started?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: I was not at all interested in politics at the time, so I don't know how the conflicts started.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the blockade of Bijeljina carried out by the Green Berets and the Patriotic League, that is, Muslim extremists, just before the conflict broke out? Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: No. All I know is that Arkan caused the conflicts in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that, at the invitation of local leadership, he arrived only after the blockade had been set up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: No. If there were legal authorities there, why would they call on him with his paramilitary units which were illegal?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you'd probably have to ask them and not me. But this is a fact I'm putting forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No good asking this witness about it. He's not from -- he's not from Bijeljina, he's not interested in politics, this is yet another semantic debate. So let's move on. Ask him about Janja. He knows about that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I know what I have to ask him about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. 1486, you say that Janja was under a blockade. Did you personally see some sort of blockade of Janja?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: During two or three days on the Bijeljina side, I saw personally three tanks with their barrels pointing towards Janja. This was the period when the population of Janja could not leave Janja in any direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: According to information I have, no inhabitant of Janja or Bijeljina was ever prohibited from leaving that area, nor were any permits necessary for this. Is this correct or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Permits were needed by all able-bodied male citizens of Janja who had to go to Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. 1486. You have just said that there was no activity by the JNA and that the JNA did not participate in these events. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How can you say, then, that the JNA blockaded you when you saw, which I doubt, three tanks on a farm near Janja? There were soldiers all over Yugoslavia, on the entire territory.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: That's correct. But who was it who had tanks in that period?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the JNA certainly had to have tanks in that period. And in that period, as you know, the JNA was on its own territory, the territory of Yugoslavia. Many units of the JNA were deployed all over Yugoslavia, but they did not take action against anyone. In the events that you speak of, did the JNA do anything at all that could be described as violent?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, on that day Bosnia was already recognised, and you speak of the presence of units of the JNA which then had tanks. How could the JNA be on that territory?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. 1486, you know that, unfortunately, tragically, Bosnia was recognised prematurely on the 16th of April, the date that Hitler bombed Yugoslavia in 1941.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're certainly getting a very long way from the evidence. Now, come back to Janja or we'll stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Have we cleared this up? Was Janja blocked or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Yes, it was, for two days, two or three days, because the population could not go anywhere. They could not leave Janja at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was Janja surrounded by JNA tanks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: I saw only three tanks on one side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it was not encircled. What, then, did this blockade consist in, that you speak of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Limited movement of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who limited your movement? It had to be some forces that limited your movement. Someone had to have ordered you not to move around. Who was it who limited your movement? Who was present in Janja to limit your movement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: There was a checkpoint on the road leading from Janja to Bijeljina and another one leading to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who manned these checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Some sort of forces, but I can't tell you exactly who they were because I didn't even attempt to go to those places, to see who these people were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that Arkan came to Janja and called on the people to hand over their weapons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember - at least, that's what my information says - that he was accompanied by the deputy commander of the traffic police who was an inhabitant of Janja, Mehmed Gruhonjic. Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: This was ten years ago, so I couldn't give you a precise answer now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that there were only a few of them, only a few men accompanying him, that there was no unit there, that there had been no fighting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: There were four or five men escorting him, escorting Arkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Four or five men? And according to you and as my information says, he made a speech, he stayed about a quarter of an hour, and then he left. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct, I have noted down that you said that not a single bullet was fired by the Muslims. That's what you said, didn't you, Mr. 1486?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was a single bullet fired by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Not in that period, not on the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So not a single bullet was fired by anyone; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Yes. But later on there were problems. So this refers only to that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So when was this later, as you say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: The problems started in late 1992 and continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the problems started in late 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, let's clarify this. Did someone shoot at somebody? Did someone fire on someone? Was someone killed in Janja?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Yes, there were such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's be very precise about this and clarify it fully because my information says the opposite, that nobody was killed in Janja. And secondly, is it correct that the problems started only when refugees began to arrive in Janja from various places from which Serbs were fleeing under pressure from Muslim forces and the crimes committed there? Is this correct or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: It's correct that problems were caused by Serbs arriving in Janja and taking over our housing and taking our property.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. 1486, is it correct that problems were not caused by the citizens of the neighbouring villages or your fellow villagers of -- people from Bijeljina but refugees fleeing from places where they had been under threat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: That's correct. Most of the problems were caused by people arriving in Janja and settling there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I assume that your neighbours and the citizens of Bijeljina had no need to move into your houses because they were already living there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So these had to be people arriving from other areas from which they had been expelled.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, if that's correct, is it also correct that this huge mass of refugees inevitably produced a situation which was suitable or conducive to various sorts of criminal actions under such circumstances?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: That's correct. These problems --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Give me a specific example. You say that a policeman confiscated your house. Where did this policeman come from? Was he from Bijeljina? Was he from your neighbourhood? Or did he arrive from somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: He arrived from somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where did he come from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: From Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So from Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So he was a refugee.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to clarify that what was happening was a result of a large wave of refugees and of events that occurred at that time. Tell me, then, you said that some people had to go to the army in order not to lose their jobs. According to my information, regardless of whether they were Serbs or Muslims, according to a decision issued by the authorities, every citizen had a choice: Either they could join the army or they could accept a work assignment, which meant that he would have to work for a certain number of hours. And this applied to both Serbs and Muslims. Are you aware of this, Mr. 1486?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Yes, I'm fully aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So there was no discrimination in this respect between Serbs and Muslims; isn't that correct, Mr. 1486?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Yes. But many Serbs did join the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But they also had a choice and many decided not to go into the army but, rather, to accept a work assignment, and everyone followed his own decision; isn't that correct, Mr. 1486?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let's proceed. Let's move on. In relation to these events, is it correct that there were various barricades in Bijeljina and the surrounding villages throughout this area and that they were set up by both Serbs and Muslims who were afraid of each other?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: I have no information as to what was going on outside Janja.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But the conflict between the Serbs and the neighbouring villages and the inhabitants of Janja, there was never any such conflict; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: That's correct. There never was such a conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So your answer is yes, there was never any conflict between the Serbs in the surrounding villages and the Muslims in Janja.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that Janja was entirely surrounded by Serbian villages?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Yes, that is also correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And there was a conflict between the Muslims in Janja and the inhabitants of the surrounding villages.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: No, there never was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the only problem you ever had was the problem with this wave of refugees, when speaking of the kind of people who caused problems for you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to skip a number of questions that I have here because your testimony is being limited to Janja. You spoke about the mosques.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: According to my information, of the three mosques, two were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: The third mosque that you mention was under construction, and that third mosque was not destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So of the three, two were destroyed. And that was also done by those people who came into the area, refugees, for some sort of revenge or retaliation because they were bitter about something. I can't go into their reasons. But without a doubt, it wasn't done by the authorities or the inhabitants of the surrounding villages around Janja; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: The destruction of the mosques was carried out at night when the curfew was in force. Now, who destroyed the mosques, I really wouldn't venture to say at this point, whether it was the refugees or the locals. So that was actually done by somebody who knew how to do it, because the surrounding houses were not destroyed as well and they were very close to the mosque, so it was done by professionals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But do you happen to know that not only the authorities of Serbia but the authorities of Republika Srpska as well on several occasions publicly condemned the desecration of religious sites, mosques, churches, and the like, and publicly called this serious crimes, said that these things were serious crimes. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Well, not much mention was made of that. Perhaps once, quite superficially, just a few words to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, how far this was publicised, I don't know. But do you know whether a single mosque was ever destroyed in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Well, I haven't got any information about that at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said in your statement - let me just find it - but it's not a long statement, and I'm sure you'll be able to remember this portion of it - that the pound authority was 100 per cent Serb and the people of different ethnic groups were dismissed from their jobs. And you say that doctors had to work, to do menial jobs like cleaning the streets. You said that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Yes. They had a work assignment which was to clean the streets and parks and see to the area around these streets as well. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. B-1486, I'm going to read some information out to you and you tell me if it's correct or not. First, none of those doctors were dismissed from their jobs; and second, the work assignment, work obligation, any kind of work assignment, as you know full well, in the former Yugoslavia -- for example, I myself took part in some of them and you probably did too. When a settlement was being put into order, we would all go out and take part in seeing that the settlement and residential area we lived in was nicely kept. It wasn't -- nobody was forced to do so. Directors would do so. Generals would do so. Housewives and children would take part in this general cleaning-up drive in their residential houses and blocks. Is that what you're thinking about? Is that what you have in mind, or do you really mean to say that somebody forced the doctors of Bijeljina to clean the streets?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: This was forced work. The competent authorities forced people to engage in this work assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the competent authorities were not ethnically purely Serb but the competent authorities had members who were Serbs and Muslims alike? Are you aware of that or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: After the events which took place in Bijeljina, there were very few Muslims who stayed on in the authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, do you know the enormous number of Muslims who were even in the army of Republika Srpska and were commanding officers, held high-ranking positions in that army, they were also directors and managers too. Are you aware of that? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Well, I don't have much information along those lines, but I did hear that in Bijeljina there were certain commanders who assumed command positions in the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, as you say that some respectable people were dismissed from their jobs and doctors, instead of doing their own work, had to clean the streets, I have here several names. For example, Dr. Nedzad Havic, Dr. Senada Gordic Nakicevic, Dr. Nijara Opalic, Dr. Sureta Kadric, Dr. Tikvesa Amra. Throughout the war, the whole time, they were engaged in their job at the Bijeljina hospital. They did their work there. Are you aware of that? Do you know about that? What did you say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: The names of those doctors, or rather, lady doctors, are not familiar to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And are you familiar with this: That throughout the war, Dr. Hasagic worked all the time. He's a well-respected physician and also Muslim.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did you say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: I said that's true, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So nobody dismissed him from his job or made him clean streets.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Not him, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the names I read out to you, you don't know about them, they don't ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned a doctor by the name of Hajrudin Kadric. There was no such doctor in Bijeljina. All the names that I read out who are Muslim and worked throughout the war, you say you don't know those doctors and then you mentioned this Dr. Kadric that doesn't exist. Perhaps there's a person of that name but he never worked at the medical centre in Bijeljina as a doctor. So where did you get that name from? Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: It's a well-known doctor, and he used to work in Janja too. Later on, he worked in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, what happened to him? Was he dismissed from his job?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Dismissed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's what you claim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milosevic, you've had rather more than the Prosecution had. Do you want more time with this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, yes, Mr. May, I do indeed because it's quite clear here that we have to clear up what the witness has been saying and claiming. As you can see, I'm asking questions and limiting them to Janja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll consider the position. Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ten minutes more.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know what I can do in ten minutes, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can get on with it and ask some more questions. Yes, let's get on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ten minutes is much too short, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. B-1486, you're not only talking about Janja, then, when you mention this Dr. Hasagic. You have confirmed that nobody dismissed him from his job, that he continued working, and then you go on to speak about Bijeljina and Hajrudin Kadric and you say that somebody dismissed him from his job there. So you're talking about things that weren't going on in Janja, actually; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Yes, I do, and they had a work assignment. They had their own work assignment working in their own workplace.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask that the last question be redacted. I believe it will provide sufficient information to reveal the identity of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, then. Now, Bijeljina is the centre here and this won't identify the witness because everybody goes to a department store, what I'm going to ask now. I'm going to give you some names of Muslims who worked in the department store throughout. Halida Alic, Senada Pasalic, Fadila Ramic, Hamdija Racevic [phoen], Dzemila Obradovic, and so on and so forth. Do you know that those people worked throughout that time at the department store; they went on working?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Up until what date, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Throughout the war, all the time. In 1991 and 1992 and 1993 and 1994 and 1995. I don't know; all the time. That's what my information tells me, the whole time. Nobody touched them. Did they have a work assignment to work in the department store?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, about 200 inhabitants remained in Janja at the end of September 1994 of the more than 10.000 inhabitants that had lived there previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you that. An enormous number of inhabitants did relocate, fleeing from the war. Serbia had several hundred thousand refugees from all parts, including 70.000 Muslims from Bosnia-Herzegovina itself. So about that population exodus and movement, I'm not asking you about that. And you say that that happened sometime in 1994. So that's not something I'm addressing here. But what I'm asking you is this: Do you know that the PD of Semberija at Novo Selo, near Bijeljina, that a large number of Muslims lived there? Do you know Alija Omerovic? He was captured, for example, by the opposite side and exchanged and is still living and working there. Alija Dragic is another case in point. Zijad Mekic, do you know him? Sead Tikves, another one, head of the vegetable plant branch. He -- this one was slaughtered by the extremists. Muharem Risanovic, Rifet Delic, Sadik Dedic. Do any of those names ring a bell? Neda Pesavic [phoen]? He had a Ph.D. in agriculture and was one of the managers there. Alija Pahatic [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's no way the witness can answer all this -- a long list. Now, you can ask -- ask one question and make it simple.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What I'm asking you is, in general terms, do you know anything about these people, the people who worked there and lived there, and who, as you can see, had problems with the other side? Do you know anything about that and about them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about that and I'm not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, for example, that Pasaga Halilovic was the general manager of the company called Duvan?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Yes, he was. And he was also one of the commanders in the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, do you think he was forced to be the general manager and one of the commanders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Well, for him to be a general manager, he would have had to have been in the Army of Republika Srpska as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, he was the general manager there before and now and he was not in the Republika Srpska Army.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: But he was during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that bears out what I'm saying. But let's not move on further from here. Tell me this, please, just to clarify one more point: You mentioned a man named Vojkan.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Right. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And this man was in charge of the exchanges. I'm now going to ask you to give me a very detailed and specific answer as to whether my piece of information on the subject is correct. This is it: According to my piece of information, this is what it was about: It was Vojkan Djurkovic, the man in question - he was a criminal, in fact - from the village of Velino Selo, near Bijeljina. And according to my data, he went about looting and took people off, and he was arrested on several occasions because of that and criminal reports were filed against him, charges were brought against him. According to what it says here, my information, he would represent himself falsely as being a member of some kind of exchange commission, which wasn't true. There was a regular exchange commission in Bijeljina at that time, and the head of that commission was Major Ljubo Mitrovic, whereas this other one, the one you mention --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's enough for the witness -- for the witness to be able to answer. B-1486, can you help as to this Vojkan? What's suggested is that he was a criminal and he went around looting and representing himself as a member of the exchange commission. Can you help as to whether that's right or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I personally know that Vojkan organised convoys for the population to leave Janja and go to Tuzla, for their displacement from Janja to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. What about this other piece of information that I have received and people guarantee that this is true: Do you know that in respect of the exchanges, Major Ljubo Mitrovic was in charge in Janja throughout the whole time? He was the official commission. No Vojkan existed in any position of authority.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: The population of Janja didn't go up for an exchange. It undertook to leave the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who forced you to leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Before Janja -- before the exodus of Janja took place, there was a number of cases during the night when the population of Janja were taken off, their houses stormed, and the inhabitants taken off during the night. Whole families, in fact, would be taken away. And then this was a way of intimidating the population and instilling fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, fear was quite certainly a motive for leaving areas; fear of war and war operations, fear of criminals, refugees, and so on. Fear is always a motive, but that is the case with all refugees, regardless of their ethnic group; isn't that so, Mr. B-1486?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Yes, that is true, but you must understand one thing: There were no war operations in Janja, and everything was taken away from us and we had no means of livelihood after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did anybody force you to leave Janja? Did anybody read out an order of any kind to you which said you, the Muslims -- this is a Muslim village, as we have established. 99 per cent of it were Muslims. Did anybody say you now have to leave your village and go? Did any person in authority ever take any measures to force you to leave Janja? Did you have to leave Janja under duress?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Nobody coerced us in any way, but the population of Janja had had all their property taken away from them and so they had to leave because of the psychological pressure exerted upon them. They had to leave their place of residence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. They left their town because of the psychological pressure. Now, what was the pressure that made them leave their homes, those who fled from Central Bosnia to take up residence in Janja? Did they leave because of similar pressure being exerted upon them? Are you aware of the fact that it was a civil war, in fact, and that everybody suffered, all three ethnic groups, ethnic communities suffered and all the citizens and inhabitants were suffering, regardless of their ethnic affiliation? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: I don't know who had to leave, under what kind of pressure, who had to leave their homes and houses, but I know personally why I myself left my home town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You've explained that to us. Now, does the name Ibro Huremovic seem familiar to you, nicknamed Ibrica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Yes, I know that name very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, he is said to have made a great contribution to mutual cooperation and trust and confidence. He is a highly respected Muslim. He was highly esteemed, and he made great contributions to avoid all the tensions, or rather, to reduce tensions as far as was possible and to have people live calmly and normally. At least, the Serb side has that to say about him. I don't know whether you share that opinion of him or not.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Yes, that is quite correct. What you have said is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is he living in Janja today too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Yes, he is, he is living in Janja today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And nobody expelled him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you must now bring your questions to an end. We'll hear one more question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm trying to select one. I did have a large number of questions for this witness, Mr. May. So this is a limiting factor. The other side over there never uses the amount of time that it says it will be using.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me just this, then, please: As we have established what was going on between the Serbs and Muslims, you claim on page 3 of your statement that you were not allowed to travel and that the furthest you could go was to Bijeljina. Did you personally, you yourself, ever have any restrictions in travelling to Bijeljina, in just going to Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: I didn't have any need to travel further than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What I was asking you was were there any restrictions in you personally travelling? Because you said that in general terms sometimes restrictions were imposed, whereas my information says that there were no restrictions at all. Now, you yourself - you're speaking about yourself personally - did you have any difficulty, any restrictions at all imposed upon you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: I could travel with special permits or passes issued by the Serb authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. My information tells me that there were no special permits or passes, that people were allowed to move around freely. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: The military department in Bijeljina did issue special passes or permits for the movement of Serbs and Muslims as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it was the military department, was it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have the answer. Yes, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Witness, you told us that Arkan addressed the people of Janja. And is it right to say that he told you that there was a new authority in the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Yes. He said that from then on the so-called Serbian authorities would be in charge in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And did he give that a name as being Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: I don't think he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: From that time, did the police start to wear new insignia on their uniform, showing "Republika Srpska"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Two or three days later, the police started wearing the new insignia, which they still wear today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And in that time, did you see soldiers also wearing the insignia of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: No, I didn't see soldiers at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm just -- I'm just looking at your statement here that says, "From time to time, Serb soldiers wearing the insignia of the Army of the Republika Srpska would come to Janja."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that did happen. But starting in June or July 1992, from then on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And when you've referred to the Serbs and the Serb authorities from then on, by that you mean Republika Srpska; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: In that period the territory bore the correct name of the SAO Semberija and Majevica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was about to put a last question which did not relate to anything to do with the previous question, and it's very brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. We gave you ten minutes more. You'd had half an hour. So you had more than -- a third more than the Prosecution. It's more than sufficient. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution is going to withdraw the video and not -- and produce it perhaps with another witness, given the technical problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But I do have a few questions to ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, if you could do so briefly, and then we should have the adjournment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Witness B-1486, Mr. Milosevic has characterised this Vojkan as a well-known criminal who committed many crimes against the population of Janja and Bijeljina. To your knowledge, was there ever any sincere attempt by the local police to impede the activity of Vojkan or to prevent him from committing crimes against the population?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic has not switched on his microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We can't hear it because you haven't put your microphone on. If you put it on, we'll listen to it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I say I have an objection because the question is not well put. I did not say only that he was a criminal, I said that he was a criminal who had been arrested on several occasions by the authorities in Bijeljina. An arrested criminal. That was my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the witness can deal with it. What he's asked is: Do you -- perhaps you could deal with this, Witness. You were asked if, to your knowledge, Vojkan was ever arrested or anything of that sort.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no special information about Vojkan. All I know personally is that he organised convoys, provided security for the vehicles, and escorted the population from Janja to Ban Brdo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milosevic asked you whether you were presented with a -- a written order or a piece of paper directing you to leave Janja. My question to you is: The population of Janja or the people that you knew in Janja, was part of the property that was taken from them implements and tools and necessary equipment that was essential for them to earn a living, to support themselves in Janja?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear the reply.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. All the farm machinery was confiscated. All the housing was confiscated. Everything was taken from the farming population.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: With respect to employment, can you estimate for the Chamber what population -- or what was the impact of the events of April 1992 on the ability of Muslim men and women to have -- to gain employment in Janja at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: A small part of the population in Janja held jobs. This was an agricultural area. Most of the people worked in towns, in Bijeljina or outside Bijeljina. And of course because their movements were restricted in this period and also because they were afraid to go to other towns, the population lost their jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You agreed with the statement by Mr. Milosevic that many of the crimes committed against the Muslim population of Janja were in fact committed by an influx of Serb refugees into the area. My question to you is: Do you have any personal knowledge or were you aware of any attempts by the local police to protect the property interest of local Muslims who remained after the takeover?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: In that period, the police did practically nothing to protect the local Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, my final question to you is: You said that the population of Janja -- or I think your exact phrase was the inhabitants of Janja was reduced from 10.000 to 200, but you did not specify the ethnicity. Can you tell us, what ethnicity were you referring to for this group of 9.800 people that left Janja?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: From late September 1994 until the end of war operations, about 200 Muslims remained in Janja.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And that's out of the original population of 10.000; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question in connection with this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. You've -- you've had your chance to cross-examine. In fact, the witness gave that evidence rather earlier. Witness -- no, we can't go on with constant re-examination -- further cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doesn't it seem to you, Mr. May, that the witness should answer the question of what happened with those 9.000 after the war; did they go back to Janja, were they killed somewhere? What happened to them after Dayton? What happened to those 9.000?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can ask the witness that. Let us ask the witness. I will ask him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You were asked about the 9.000. You heard what Mr. Milosevic said, Witness B-1486. Can you deal with what happened to the 9.000 of the population?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: About 4.000 in 1994 were practically moved to Tuzla and the surrounding area. Over 1.000 inhabitants remained in Majevica in camps and -- performing work obligation. And the remainder, through various channels, went to other countries via Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And what happened after Dayton? Can you tell us? Did any of them go back?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1486
utterances.text: About 80 per cent of the population of Janja have now returned to their homes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness B-1486, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for making yourself available to give it to the Tribunal. You are now free to go. We will adjourn --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Now, what is it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard Mr. Groome say at the beginning that he will not keep to the order of witnesses that was announced. He mentioned a witness. I have not managed to remember now. We don't know who the next witness will be. Who is the next witness? May I know, at least, before the break who the witness will be?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. We'll ask Mr. Groome that. B-104; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's B-1493. The witness that was scheduled for Thursday will be accelerated to tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But who's the next witness, is the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The witness is B-104, Your Honour. That schedule has not changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: B-104 now. And then after him?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Will be B-1493.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And then I think you said Mr. Torkildsen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Torkildsen then. Your Honour, I am informed by Ms. Wee that there's a new witness schedule that will be distributed at the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll adjourn now. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If you'd like to sit down.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I ask that we go briefly into private session so the pseudonym sheet can be placed on the overhead projector. I'm informed that's the only way to keep it confidential.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Witness B-104, in order to facilitate and hasten your testimony here today, were you asked to -- with a member of the OTP staff, to write a chart indicating or summarising your educational background, as well as your professional experience?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask that the registry personnel on site please show the witness Prosecution Exhibit 424, tab 2.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And my question is: Is this a summary of your educational and professional background?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: That your writing at the bottom of that document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: I want to begin by asking you: Were you a member of the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And was there a time that you were assigned in Nis, Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And were you attached to the air force brigade in Nis?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Can I ask you to describe for the Chamber briefly what individual units together made up the air force brigade in Nis.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: It consisted of anti-armour helicopter, a unit in Kraljevo, a helicopter transport unit in Nis, and -- excuse me, in Kraljevo, there was an anti-armour and a transport in -- and in Nis, and there was also a reconnaissance unit.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: What time of aircraft was used in the unit that was responsible for reconnaissance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Gazelle helicopters.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Were you assigned to one of these units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Which unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: I was in the unit in Nis, the Reconnaissance and Transport Unit, and I flew Gazelle helicopters.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: What was the name of that unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: As far as I remember --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We have lost the sound.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Can you please repeat your answer. We lost your answer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: This unit, as far as I can recall, was called the 712th Anti-armour Helicopter Squadron.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Was it known by another name as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: It was also known as the Skorpions.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: What were your duties and responsibilities with the 712th helicopter unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: I flew as a technician. I worked on maintaining the helicopters. That was my basic assignment in these units.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And can you tell us who was your superior officer when you were in the 712th helicopter unit.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: My first superior officer was the commander of the squadron, and his name was Miodrag Petricevic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Now, can you in a sentence or two just summarise for the Chamber the procedure that was followed when you were paid as a member of this unit.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: When I received per diem for my work, I had to sign a document with the date, the amount, and my signature had to be affixed to that document.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that the registry personnel on site show the witness Prosecution Exhibit 424, tab 3. Sir, I'd ask you to take a look at this document and ask you: Do you recognise this as being a document similar to the document you signed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And so the record is clear, you do not recognise any of the particular names on tab 3 that's before you now; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Now, B-104, I'd like to draw your attention to the winter and spring of 1993, and I want to ask you: Were you assigned as part of your official duties to go to a place called Bajina Basta?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: I will ask you to refer to a map at the conclusion of your testimony, but could I ask you at this stage just to orient the Chamber regarding where, generally speaking, Bajina Basta is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: This is a place in Serbia near the border with the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, by the River Drina.
