utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: If one were to cross the Drina and enter Bosnia, what part of Bosnia would one be in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: The place was called Skelani. That's the first town on the Bosnian side.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And do you know what municipality Skelani is in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: I believe it was part of the municipality of Srebrenica, but I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Can you summarise for the Chamber what it was you were called to do in Bajina Basta.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: The first time I went to Bajina Basta, it was to transport a wounded soldier from the parachute brigade in Nis. He had been wounded in the operations around Srebrenica. I was to transport him to the military hospital in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And can you summarise for us what you did on subsequent occasions in Bajina Basta.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: On subsequent occasions when I went to Bajina Basta, I transported some sort of materiel. I can't remember exactly what. Then it was to reconnoitre and things like that.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you come to learn that during that period there was an operation being organised out of Bajina Basta?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And did you come to learn who it was that was in charge of that operation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: From what people were saying and talking with people who were there in Bajina Basta, the person in charge was Mr. Franko or Frenki, which was his nickname.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you know his last name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it was Mr. Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And the operation, in what geographic location was the operation primarily being deployed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: The operation was being deployed in the location around Srebrenica, which means between Bajina Basta and Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Now, were there two locations in Bajina Basta of significance for your testimony here today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Before I ask you specific questions about those locations, can you just briefly tell us or identify each of the two locations.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: They were locations -- first of all, there was the hotel, which is where they were accommodated, where they slept and spent time. And the other place was a house which was a kind of mini command centre.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Now, you've identified yourself as being a member of the 712th helicopter unit. During the times that you were in Bajina Basta, were there other members of the 712th helicopter unit also present?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Were there other members of the Yugoslav People's Army or the Army of Yugoslavia, as it was known at this time, present in Bajina Basta, also participating in this operation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Again, before I ask you specific questions about each of those units, would you please at this stage simply identify the names of the different units.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: The units of the Army of Yugoslavia who were in those areas and took part in the operations were my own unit, the unit of which I was a member, the helicopter unit; then there was the parachute brigade from Nis; and there is also the guards brigade from Belgrade. All these were parts of units, not an entire unit.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Let me ask you about the parachute brigade. Do you know the full formal name of that parachute brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: It was the 63rd Parachute Brigade.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And the guards brigade that you referred to, can you tell us, if you know, the full formal name of that brigade -- that brigade and from where that brigade originated.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Would you repeat that, please. I didn't hear the question.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: You've mentioned a portion of a unit of the guards brigade was also present. My question to you is: Can you tell us the full formal name of that guards brigade and tell us where they were based, if you know.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: That was the 72nd Guards Brigade, and they were located in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Now, in addition to these members of the Yugoslav army, were there members of other armed groups that you saw in Bajina Basta, also participating in this operation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Can you please identify them for us at this stage.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: They were members of the police from the Republic of Serbia. Then there were also members of the so-called Wolves from the Drina. That was the name of the unit.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: I want to draw your attention once again to the hotel. Can you please describe where the hotel was located in the town and for what purpose it was used.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: The hotel was located in the centre of town itself, and it was used, as I've already said, to accommodate people during the day and night.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: During the times you were in Bajina Basta, can you estimate for us to what capacity was the hotel? Was it fully filled, half-filled; can you please estimate that for us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: While I was in Basta, the hotel was more or less full, full of the people who took part in these operations.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And can you approximate for us the number of people that would be in the hotel when it was full?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Well, the number would be about 100 people. I never counted them, so I can't say exactly.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Now, the people that you saw in this hotel, were they dressed in civilian clothes or were they dressed in uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: All of them were dressed in uniforms.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to now describe the different uniforms that you saw there, and I'm going to ask you to describe them as the first uniform, the second uniform, so it's clear to us what parts of the uniform belonged to which individual uniform. So would you please describe for us what uniforms you observed -- what you remember about the uniforms that you observed there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Well, it was like this: One of the uniforms that I saw around was the type that I wore, which was a camouflage uniform of the Army of Yugoslavia. Then the next type of uniform that could be seen there was a camouflage uniform, the type of uniform that the police wore of the Republic of Serbia. Then there were black uniforms, worn by certain members of the Wolves from the Drina. And then there were some other ones which were olive-green, olive-drab uniforms, also worn by these Wolves from the Drina.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Now, you've mentioned two different types of camouflage uniform, one like the one you wore and one like one worn by the police. Can you give us a little bit more detail to help distinguish between those two camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: The uniform that I myself wore was predominantly grey or olive-green, a greeny-grey colour, whereas the other uniform worn by the policemen and people who were there was predominantly blue.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: In addition to these uniforms, did any members or any of the people there wear insignias that you can recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: In addition to the uniforms, they wore insignia, the Drina Wolves insignia patches, and also those of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that you look at the monitor before you, and there will be an exhibit displayed for you, and that is Exhibit 349.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, when we originally were scheduled to have this witness testify, the register -- the registry had reserved tab 7 for this particular patch. So perhaps that would assist the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: I would ask you to take a look at the monitor before you and ask you, do you recognise the patch that you see before you? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And can you tell us what you recognise it to be.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: This is the patch worn by members of the unit called Wolves from the Drina, or Drina Wolves.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Now, during your time in Bajina Basta, did you have an opportunity to speak with many of the men that were there in uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Were you able to identify their place of origin by their accents?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Well, in principle, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Can you tell us what, if any, locations you were able to identify by the accent of the people that you spoke with.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Judging by their accent, I concluded that they were from Serbia, Montenegro, and Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Can you please describe the context in which you saw these men at the hotel. Can you describe the types of things you would see them doing.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Those people were dressed in uniforms. Just like me, they had probably come there to work on certain assignments in the area.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And did you see anything which led you to believe that they were actively engaged in carrying out assignments as opposed to being there for recreational purposes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Can you please describe what your observations were.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Well, I observed that they would change frequently. Some would go; others would come in. And also when they returned, when they came back from the field, they would be very tired and dirty looking. So this led me to conclude that they had been in the field and were engaged in war operations.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you come to learn where it was, generally speaking, that they were engaged in war operations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Generally speaking, they were engaged in war operations in the territory of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Now, the other location you mentioned that was of significance was a place you referred to as a mini command centre. Again, I would ask you to describe where was this located in the town and describe it in a bit more detail.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: It was in the centre of town. It was a house. As far as I remember, it had an upper storey. Inside there was a sort of office, a quite large office, with some maps in it and radio communications devices, that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: How many times were you on the inside of this command post?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Well, two or three times.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: While you were in Bajina Basta, were there -- or did you see vehicles there that you believed were being used in part for this operation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Can you please describe those vehicles and where they were customarily parked.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: The vehicles were white jeeps, of the Defender type, and they were usually parked in front of the hotel or in front of the mini command centre, so-called.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: You said that you were inside the mini command centre two or three times. Can I ask you to tell us about the first time you were in that command centre.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: The first time I went to that mini command centre I went because I had -- needed somewhere to spend the night in Bajina Basta, in a hotel, and I met a girl there and they said that she was Mr. Frenki's secretary. And she phoned Mr. Frenki up to ask him whether I could spend the night in the hotel.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Can I ask you to describe her physical appearance as best you can recall.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: She was a young woman with long black hair. She wore a uniform.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did it appear to you in this command centre that she had her own designated work area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: What was the purpose of your first -- I withdraw that. You said that the purpose of your first trip to Bajina Basta was to do a medevac. Can you tell us a little bit more detail about how you received that assignment and where precisely you were to airlift the injured soldier from.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: I was given the assignment in Nis, and we set out, I myself and the pilot, and then the commander of the parachute brigade of Nis and an officer who, as I was told, was an officer for intelligence work in the parachute brigade. So we left for Bajina Basta. We dropped down at the stadium of Bajina Basta. And the two officers were with us. They went to collect the injured person, and they stayed overnight up there too. I had to go to the hotel and consult my colleagues, who were staying in the hotel, as to where I was going to spend the night. The next day they came back, and they weren't able to carry out their assignment because of the bad weather conditions. The wounded man was transported in a car.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Was the original intention to evacuate this injured soldier by helicopter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And where precisely was this injured soldier to be -- to be airlifted from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: He was supposed to be airlifted from the hill or, rather, mountain, I don't know which it is, but the name was Osmace. But we weren't able to land on that hill, so he had to be evacuated by car to Bajina Basta and from there transported to Belgrade by us.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And the location where he was to be evacuated from, in what republic was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Were you informed that this member of the Yugoslav army, of the 63rd Parachute Brigade, had been injured in an official capacity in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: How long were you in Bajina Basta on this first trip to that area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Roughly about a week. Five, six, or seven days. I don't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you make subsequent trips to Bajina Basta?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: On some of those subsequent trips, did you actually see a person you came to know as Frenki Simatovic there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: You've mentioned members from three units of the Yugoslav army. During your time there, did you form an opinion regarding their relationship to that of Frenki Simatovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: In a way, Frenki was the superior to all of us over there.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Can you please tell us specifically what it was you observed or heard that led you to that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: In principle, Frenki would issue the orders and people would salute Frenki in a way when he was giving out orders.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you yourself personally observe Frenki issuing instructions or orders to the members of the Yugoslav army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Well, not personally. I didn't notice him issue orders personally to members of the Army of Yugoslavia. There was always someone there who was higher up, a high-ranking officer who would communicate with the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: When you were there, did you ever personally see members of the Yugoslav army salute Frenki Simatovic as they would salute a superior in their own ranks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: With respect to the other units that you mentioned, police units from the Republika Srpska, and the Drina Wolves, did you form an opinion regarding Frenki Simatovic and those units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: You mean with respect to those units. Mr. Frenki's relationship was superior, and I did notice them saluting him.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And did you ever hear him -- were you ever present when he issued a direct order to a member of those units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: On a couple of occasions, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: During the time that you were present in Bajina Basta, did you consider Frenki Simatovic to be a superior to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: In a way, yes. But not -- but generally speaking, no.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: When you say "in a way, yes," can you please describe what you mean by that answer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Well, what I mean is that Frenki was in charge of everything going on in Bajina Basta. And in view of the fact that he was in charge of that entire operation, we were a unit which came under his command. However, as I've already explained to you, there was always a commanding officer with us who was in charge of communication between Mr. Frenki and the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: If Frenki Simatovic wanted to deploy your helicopter unit in a particular way, can you describe for us the procedure that would be followed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Frenki would usually talk to us about the ways and means in which the unit could be deployed, what a helicopter can do. And then he would reach an agreement and the officer who was there would issue orders to us.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: The officer that you're referring to as directly issuing the order to you, was he a member of the Yugoslav army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And was it the same person throughout the times -- or the different times that you went to Bajina Basta?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Those people would change from time to time. It wasn't always the same person, one and the same man.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Was there ever a time that this officer was not present and orders were communicated to your helicopter unit by another means?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Can you please describe.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: On a couple of occasions people would relay -- people that we recognised there would relay orders to us. And it was a local man, usually, from whom we would be given instructions as to what we were supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: This local man, did you come to learn his name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Yes. I remember his nickname, and his nickname was Max.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Was he ever in the company of an assistant?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Very often.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And if you can, please tell us the name of that assistant.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: His name was Nedjo.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Now, this person that you've referred to as Max, was he a member or could you identify to us whether he was a member of one of the units that you've described for us.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: He was a member of the Drina Wolves unit.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And during your time there, did you ever make any observations regarding how he interacted with Frenki Simatovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: I noticed that his relationship with Frenki was such that Frenki was his superior.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And can you please tell us the precise observations you made that led you to that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: I noted in concrete terms that Frenki was issuing orders to him and that he saluted Frenki.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Now, the uniform that you wore when you arrived in Bajina Basta, did it ordinarily or did it in fact have emblems and insignias which would identify you as a member of the Yugoslav army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Yes, it did have insignia on it.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Were you ever given an instruction with respect to the insignias and emblems that would identify you as a member of the Yugoslav army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Can you please describe the circumstances regarding that instruction.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: When I arrived in Bajina Basta, this gentleman, the man whose nickname was Max, would say to me or tell us to take off the insignia of the Yugoslav army and that the flag of Republika Srpska -- or if he told us to put them on, or the Drina Wolves insignia, we were supposed to do that.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Were you ever informed about the purpose behind switching identifying emblems?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Nobody told us exactly, but I concluded that the purpose of the switching of insignia was to conceal the fact that the Army of Yugoslavia was participating in these operations.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Now, when you returned from this first trip, your first visit to Bajina Basta, were you able to take -- return in your helicopter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you returned to Nis and were -- you were given an instruction regarding insignias on the helicopter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what instruction you were given with respect to the insignias on the helicopter.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: With respect to the insignia on the helicopter, my colleagues and I were instructed to take the helicopters to the workshop where the insignia of the Army of Yugoslavia would be removed from them.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Was there anything else that could identify the helicopter removed from it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: The large numbers of the helicopters were removed and small numbers were placed there instead, numbers that could not be seen from the ground when the helicopter was up in the air, and a small round flag was put on the -- on the back part of the helicopter.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And can you please describe the small round flag that was put on the back of the helicopter.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: The small round flag was the flag of Yugoslavia but without the five-pointed star.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you some questions about some of the specific units that you've referred to in your testimony here today. The first unit I would like to deal with is the 63rd Parachute Brigade. Is it true that you saw members of that brigade in Bajina Basta?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Chamber to the extent you're able what kind of operations and what kind of training did members of the 63rd Parachute Brigade have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: The 63rd Parachute Brigade went through a special kind of training, as did all parachute units everywhere in the world.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did they receive any other specialised training, to your knowledge, aside from parachute training?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: In the description of their training, there were various kinds of training, such as jumping out of a plane, jumping out of a helicopter, warfare under impossible conditions, impossible for ordinary units of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I'd ask that we go into private session for a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: The next unit I would like to draw your attention to are the Drina Wolves. Did you ever have a conversation with the two people you've identified as Max and Nedjo with respect to who it was that was their superior?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Yes. I did have conversations with them.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And who did they tell you was their superior?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: They said Mr. Frenki was their superior.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: In your conversations with them, did they describe for you or tell you the original name of their unit, what it was called before they were known as the Drina Wolves?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: They told me that they were referred to as Knindze.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you recall the names of other members of this unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: No, I can't recall their names at the moment.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Were there people of that unit that appeared to you to have some type of rank or supervisory capacity over other men in the unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: In principle, there were no ranks. But you could notice there were individuals who had certain assignments. You could see that by the way they treated others, others whose assignments were more ordinary.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Can you tell us the names of some of those individuals?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, there was a gentleman there called Njegos. Then I remember there was a gentleman they called Rajo Bozovic.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Njegos, did you learn what area of responsibility he had?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: As far as I could see, Njegos was in charge of a unit that was stationed in a hotel at Mount Tara.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Rajo Bozovic, can you describe for us how frequently you would see him.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Every time he came to Bajina Basta I would see him.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And under what circumstances would you see him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: I would see him in uniform, which meant that he was doing something there.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Based on your observations, did you form an impression regarding his relationship to that of the other men of the Drina Wolves? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: I saw that in a way he was superior to the others.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And can you describe for us your specific observations that led you to that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Specifically, I know that they respected him and they said he was in charge of parts of those units.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you came to learn that there was a group of prisoners also incorporated into that unit of the Drina Wolves?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Can you please describe how it was you learnt that information.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: There was a gentleman there whom they called Pacov, which means "rat," as far as I could remember. And when we were sitting in the hotel, people told me that he had been in prison in Kosovo and that Mr. Frenki got him out of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you ever have a conversation with Frenki's secretary regarding prisoners present in Bajina Basta?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Can you please summarise that for us.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: This was in fact on that occasion when this girl told me that the man had been in prison in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Now, one of the other units that you've described for us here today is the -- I believe you said the 72nd Guards Brigade from Belgrade. Can you tell us a bit more about that unit.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: According to my personal knowledge, this was a special purpose unit and I think it was established primarily for providing security for Tito while he was still alive. They were Tito's escort or bodyguard.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Approximately how many men from this unit did you have occasion to see in Bajina Basta?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: I can't recall the exact number, but I saw members of that unit there.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: In addition to the units that you've described here today, were there other helicopters that you saw in Bajina Basta, and if so, did you learn from where they came?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: There were other helicopters there. They were MI-8 helicopters, and they were at Mount Tara. They came from Nis.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Any other aircraft that you can recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: I didn't see any other aircraft. There were Gazelle helicopters and MI-8 helicopters.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Without going to -- into the detail in open session, did you during one of your trips to Bajina Basta fly a mission into Bosnia, into the municipality of Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask that we go into private session for the next few questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask that tab 4 of Prosecution Exhibit 424 be placed on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: B-104, you have a copy of this exhibit there with you on site. I would ask you to describe --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: I didn't hear your question.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: I'm placing Prosecution Exhibit 424, tab 4, on a projector so that those of us in the courtroom can see it. I would ask that the registry personnel down there show you a copy of the same exhibit. And when you have had an opportunity to look at it, can you tell us, do you recognise what it is?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [No microphone]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And I would ask that it be placed on the overhead projector down on site. And if possible, to zoom out. If we could zoom out some more, please. Just a bit more.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise this particular map?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And the markings on this map, who made them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And is that your handwriting on the upper left corner of the map?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And did you indicate some of the locations you've testified about here today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: I'd ask you to use a pencil or a pointer and just point to the different markings you made and identify them to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: This is Bajina Basta. This is Skelani, Bratunac, Osmace.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Can I ask you to hold the pointer on Osmace for a minute. Please go to the next mark.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Zeleni Jadar.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: I'd ask you now just to help orient the Chamber, would you please trace the border between Republic of Serbia and Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: The border runs through this part here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is Zeleni Jadar the name of a river?

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Judge Kwon has asked you whether Zeleni Jadar is the name of a river or a location. Can you please answer that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: It's a place, a hill.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you look at the page 33 of Exhibit 336, top right corner, Zeleni Jadar looks like the name of a river or name of a hill. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The witness is saying hill, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm not familiar myself enough with the geography.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: During the times that you went to Bajina Basta, did you become aware of other units or other helicopter units also going into Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And would you speak with these men regarding what they were doing in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And what was it that they told you that they were doing in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Well, they were doing the same thing I was doing. The helicopter units were -- had the same purpose as my own.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: In addition to the missions that you've already described, did you on other occasions transport Frenki Simatovic between Belgrade and Bajina Basta?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: I flew him from Bajina Basta to Belgrade and back.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have between five and ten minutes more of questions. I don't know when the Court is intending on breaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You may as well continue until the end, and then we'll break.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Can you please describe the circumstances under which you transported Frenki Simatovic between Belgrade and Bajina Basta.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: I transported him just as I would any other passenger.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Was --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: From Belgrade to Bajina Basta -- or rather, from Bajina Basta to Belgrade and back.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Was it part of your official duties to transport members of the armed services in your helicopter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Where would you pick up Frenki Simatovic in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At Banjica. That is a place close to Belgrade. Or rather, it's in town.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: On one occasion, did you become aware of a mission of several helicopters that were being sent to the Visegrad area of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: I learnt about an assignment, a mission that the helicopters were supposed to carry out.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And where was that mission to take place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: It was supposed to take place in the vicinity of Visegrad, near the dam there.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you had an informal meeting with Frenki Simatovic during which the capabilities of your aircraft were discussed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Without telling us who was present for the moment, can you please summarise what Frenki Simatovic inquired of you and the other people at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: He wanted to know of the characteristic features of my helicopter, what the helicopter could carry, how much weight it could carry, whether it could carry machine-guns or not, rifles, whether the helicopter could be shot from. Those were the kinds of questions he asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I ask that we go into private session for the next series of questions.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Sir, my final question for you today is: All of the activities that you've described for us, that you were involved in in Bajina Basta, did you consider those to be part of your official duties as a member of the Yugoslav army or did you consider those to be outside of your official duties?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: I considered them to be my official duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're going to adjourn now for 20 minutes. Witness B-104, in this adjournment and any others there may be during the course of this case, don't speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over and don't let anybody speak to you about it. We'll continue your evidence in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. 104, I would like to establish first of all what your profession is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So have we cleared this point up properly as to what it said in your statement, that your group's assignment was to occupy towns, take control of towns? Your answer was that that was not what you stated and that you don't know how this came to be contained in the statement. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: I said that I didn't say that it was my task to occupy any part of town or towns themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in the next paragraph, the first paragraph on page 4, you go on to say that your group did not take part in a single armed military operation, is that right, upon your arrival in Mostar; right? "My unit was never part of any armed military action."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: In view of the fact that I lived in Mostar, my unit took part in the transportation and reconnaissance work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But your unit, as far as I understood it, did not take part in any military operations, combat operations. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: My unit in that part of the territory never took part. It never carried out any operations, or rather, it never went and shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. On page 4, in paragraph 5 you say that on several occasions you drove General Cokic from Mostar to Belgrade. And as you say that he had had meetings with General Kadijevic and received orders from him, and you say that Kadijevic was the commander-in-chief. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, tell me, where did Cokic and Kadijevic meet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: I don't know what institution they met in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you know nothing about the content of these meetings.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You assume, then, that the Federal Secretary issued orders to Cokic, the commander of the 2nd Operative Group, bypassing the then commander of the air force, whoever he was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: I don't know whether he met the commander of the air force and how the talks were conducted, but I do know he attended those meetings. Who was present, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So all that you know was that he went to meetings in Belgrade. You know nothing else.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 4 in paragraph 6 you explained the chain of command in the Mostar region in 1991 and you say that it went from Kadijevic to Cokic, who ultimately issued orders to Lazar Murisic, the brigade commander; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is how you explained the chain of command, and now you say you don't know.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: I know who was there and how the chain of command went in the Mostar region. Lazar Murisic was the commander of the air force brigade, and General Cokic was the commander of the 2nd Operational Group, and they cooperated with each other.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whenever I put the headset on, there's a squeaking noise. But when I take them off, I don't hear well. These links are not very successful.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, what military district was Mostar a part of in 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't remember. All right. And who was the commander of the air force in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't remember that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you don't remember that either. Have you heard of General Tus, General Jurevic, and so on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's suggested if you put the headset on, Mr. Milosevic, it will be better. Let's try that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic has not switched on his microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 4 -- well, when I have the headset on, I can hear my own voice very loud.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 4, in paragraph 7, you say you were ordered -- from the 9th of May, 1992 all members of the JNA had to remain in their barracks because there was a state of alert. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear your answer because this was off.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: My answer to your question was yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And why was there a state of alert?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Probably because of the events taking place in the former Yugoslavia at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that your task in May 1991 was to fly every day from Mostar to Zadar, taking information, recordings, and so on there, recorded from Yutel.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How long did you do this for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the content of those news items was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that this was a Yugoslav television station with a very strong pro-Yugoslav orientation? It was committed to Yugoslavia and to the equality of republics and peoples. Did you ever watch those news?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Yes, I did watch some.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have to carry those news items to Zadar because they could not receive Yutel in Croatia or watch it because it was pro-Yugoslav in its orientation so it could not be broadcast there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Why I had to take this to Zadar, I don't know. All I know is that I had to take those cassettes to Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on to something else. On page 4, paragraph 6 you mention a commander General Mladic and Mostar.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Explain why you mentioned this. Do you think it's unusual that the commander of a JNA corps should cooperate with commanders of other JNA units? So why do you mention this at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: I've forgotten the reason why I mentioned it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I feel that this statement should be introduced into evidence because it contradicts the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's have a copy of it, if we may.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just like many others. I don't have time to deal with all the contradictions, so let it be entered into evidence and we can discuss it later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just one moment. Any objection to it being exhibited?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I just ask that it be done under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Yes, we'll exhibit this. The next exhibit number, if we may, for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D125. Thank you, Judge Kwon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that two of your colleagues, Jugoslav Babic and Adem Tokic, with respect to Mladic's second visit in February 1992 - February 1992, therefore - that you were transported to Visegrad in a helicopter. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you claim that Jugoslav Babic, when on that same evening came back with Mladic from Visegrad said that Mladic was on a tank and that he issued the soldiers orders to advance. Is that right, according to you? Is that what you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may we deal with this in private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, before we go into private session, let me just ask you, what attack are you talking about in February 1992 led by Mladic in Visegrad? What is the attack you are talking about? Do you have any idea about what you're talking?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you want --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You're talking about February 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness go into -- let the hearing go into a private session. The witness can then answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's a nice thing to have at least something in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 5, paragraph 2, you claim that the JNA soldiers, members of the 63rd Parachute Unit, and you call them the Red Berets, that's how you refer to them, that they looted Croatian houses near the Heliodrom in Mostar. Is that what you said? Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: I did not say that they --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interruption.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Just so long as you didn't say what it says here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, let us clarify what he did say, since there's been an interruption. Witness B-104, would you just clarify what you meant by that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I meant was that the members of the 63rd Parachute Brigade went to the places around the airport and that they targeted the houses and the buildings there and that they took from these houses alcoholic beverage and that they took down the HDZ flags and put up the army flag, or rather, the flag, whichever it was at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. On page 5, you state the following, in paragraph 2, that is: "When tensions broke out between the Croatian and Yugoslav armies, there was some looting, some abandoned Croatian houses in the area around the Heliodrom in Mostar, and this was done by JNA soldiers, members of the 63rd Parachute Brigade," and in brackets you say the Red Berets. The aviation brigade commander Lazar Murisic knew about this looting without taking any actions to prevent it." So you used the word "looting" yourself, and I am asking you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope you've found it, Mr. May. "When tensions broke out," the paragraph reads.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you: Do you accuse the soldiers of the 63rd Parachute Brigade of having looted houses close to the Heliodrom or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: I'm not accusing anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, let's use another expression, then. Do you claim that the soldiers of the 63rd Parachute Brigade looted houses close to the heliport?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: I'm saying that the members of the 63rd Parachute Brigade went and took out of the houses around the heliport goods and alcohol.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago you just said "alcohol," now you add these "goods." Where did they take these goods to then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I assume they had to return to barracks, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: I didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I said I assume they had to return to barracks. How could they, then, bring the goods into the barracks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't follow what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, did you see any of the items that any one of them brought into the barracks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: I saw alcoholic drinks, and I heard that they had taken video recorders and television sets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just a minute. I asked you what you saw. You saw alcohol, alcoholic drink.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you see the video recorders and television sets you mention?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: I didn't see a single one, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you didn't see a single one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you saw the alcohol. Well, how did you get the idea into your head that this alcohol was looted from somewhere? Weren't they able to buy it in a shop in Mostar, a bottle of plum brandy, for example? Couldn't they have bought that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: In that area, there were no shops.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And don't you think that it is not in order to present lies about the looting that this elite unit allegedly did?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: I didn't say the word "loot," "pljacka."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the word was introduced here without your knowledge, was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Once again, let me say that it must be an error in the translation again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, fine. Fine. And you claim that they were called the Red Berets; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You as a soldier are well aware of the fact that the 63rd Parachute Brigade has a name. It is the 63rd Brigade. Who told you to call them the Red Berets?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We did not hear the answer, the interpreters apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's have the answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They wore berets which were red in colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. When you know all that, now tell me, who commanded this parachute unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: I don't remember the name of the person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. So you don't know that either. Now, let's move on to your story about Bajina Basta. In the examination-in-chief, in response to a question from Mr. Groome, having described the fact that these people had been put up in the hotel in Bajina Basta, in response to his question as to how many there were, if I remember, your answer was, "I don't know exactly, I didn't count them, but there were about 100." Was that your answer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So about 100 men in the hotel in Bajina Basta in Serbia, which otherwise Bajina Basta is a tourist spot; isn't that right? A tourist resort?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you say about 100.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Let me repeat once again: I didn't count them. It was a number which is an approximation. There might have been 60, 70.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. 60, 70, whatever. Let's say even 100. Now, amongst those 60 or 70 or 100 that you mentioned, you enumerated the 63rd Parachute Brigade from Nis, then you go on to state the 72nd Guards Brigade from Belgrade, and then you mention the Drina Wolves or Wolves from the Drina Unit, that is, the police of Republika Srpska. Then you said members of the police force from Serbia; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, isn't that a little too many units, too many units for just those 70 -- 60, 70, or 100 men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: They were parts of units, and they weren't all accommodated at the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. All right, Mr. 104. As a one-time JNA member yourself, do you know how many men and infantry brigade numbers of the guards brigade type, how many thousands of men such a brigade has? Do you know anything about that at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: I don't remember the numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Ah, you don't remember the numbers. You don't remember the insignia of the brigade either, because you speak about the 72nd, whereas in your statement it says 74th. Do you know which guards brigade it was at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Maybe I made a mistake in the number because a lot of time has gone past since then. But it was a guards brigade from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, a guards brigade from Belgrade, numbers several thousand men, and in those approximately 100 in which you include the Wolves, the people from Republika Srpska, and the 63rd Parachute, et cetera, you also include the guards brigade from Belgrade in all that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Let me repeat once again they were all parts of units. They were parts of units, not entire units, whole units. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you want to say some atoms of those units, don't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: I said parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, as you spoke about and you were shown here the insignia and the patches that you recognised on the sleeves of these Drina Wolves, how many Drina Wolves were there who -- which you noticed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did you say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Roughly. Give us a rough idea.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: I can't really say, not even roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were asked by Mr. Groome whether they were there for recreational purposes or whether they were on a combat assignment of any kind, and your answer was that most probably they were on a combat assignment because they came tired and dirty. So if somebody turns up tired and dirty, I assume that they come to the hotel to have rest and recreation and not to be on some combat assignment of any kind. And doesn't it seem to be to you logical that when you say they came in shifts, that they came for recuperation, to recover? Doesn't it seem to you to be the regular state of affairs or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: The hotel didn't serve the purpose of rest and recreation. It was there to accommodate people and to have them spend the night there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, is there some helicopter combat operation that was known about on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina during that period of time when you were there? Was there anything like that? According to my information, there were no combat operations effected by helicopters at that time. Do you know of any?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: I don't remember any combat operations being performed at that time, as you refer to it. I suppose that's what you mean, combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Any kind of helicopter combat operation at that time? Do you have knowledge about that or anything similar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: There were various assignments of those helicopter units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Name one combat operation on the part of a helicopter unit that you know of.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: I know about reconnaissance and reconnoitering and then the transportation of freight.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see; freight, reconnaissance. Anything else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: There were other tasks and assignments as well, judging by the stories told by men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Ah, just storied bandied about; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-104
utterances.text: Yes, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I won't go into that, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's time, Mr. Milosevic. We must adjourn now. Witness B-104, we're going to have to adjourn now. Would you be back, please, tomorrow morning to complete your evidence. Mr. Milosevic, you've got another half hour to finish your cross-examination. If you would prepare on that basis.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did I understand you correctly? Just half an hour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just half an hour. That's absolutely right. Yes. You will have then had more than the Prosecution, rather more than them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Nice has asked me to inform you -- he had some previous discussion with the Bench regarding summaries of transcript references. They have now been prepared for the parties and for the Chamber. With the Court's wish, I will hand them to the legal officer after court today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. I'm afraid I don't recollect it immediately but no doubt we will recall. Let me add something else: Tomorrow we must deal with some of the Rule 92 bis witnesses who we -- were left over from last week. So there must be time for that tomorrow morning. Very well. We'll adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: at 2.02 p.m., to be reconvened on Wednesday the 9th day of April, 2003, at 9.00 a.m.
